article_title: Toolkit to Support Capacity Building Initiatives for Strategic Learning Initiatives
citation: Emily Gardner, Emma Pottinger, Ramya Tallapragada, Alexandra Resch, Virginia Knechtel. (2021). Toolkit to Support Capacity Building Initiatives for Strategic Learning Initiatives. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/toolkit-to-support-capacity-building-initiatives-for-strategic-learning-initiatives
title: Strong equity-centered strategic learning requires equity in the learning and decision-making approach, not only in the organizational goal
description: The article argues that equity must be embedded in how an organization learns and decides, not only in what it aims for. It states that "strong equity-centered strategic learning is demonstrated when equity is considered in not only the organization's goal but also in its learning and decision-making approach." This principle distinguishes equity as a property of the improvement process itself from equity as a stated goal.
requirements: Learning and decision-making approaches in which equity is explicitly considered
target_learners: K-12 education grantee organizations
target_learning_goals: Equity-centered organizational learning and decision making
examples: The partnership articulated this criterion when defining what strong equity-centered strategic learning looks like in the CBSL initiative
key_sources: Emily Gardner, Emma Pottinger, Ramya Tallapragada, Alexandra Resch, Virginia Knechtel. (2021). Toolkit to Support Capacity Building Initiatives for Strategic Learning Initiatives. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/toolkit-to-support-capacity-building-for-strategic-learning-initiatives

article_title: Capacity Building for Strategic Learning: Findings from the Pilot Cohort
citation: Emma Pottinger, Emily Gardner, Ramya Tallapragada, Alexandra Resch, Virginia Knechtel. (2021). Capacity Building for Strategic Learning: Findings from the Pilot Cohort. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/capacity-building-for-strategic-learning-findings-from-the-pilot-cohort
title: Equity must be embedded in the learning and decision-making approach, not only in organizational goals
description: The article argues that goal statements alone are insufficient for equity-centered strategic learning. It states that "strong equity-centered strategic learning is demonstrated when equity is considered in not only the organization's goal but also in its learning and decision-making approach." Organizations should therefore examine how learning processes and decisions, not just stated goals, address equity for Black and Latino students and students experiencing poverty.
requirements: An organization adopting this principle must review both its goals and its learning and decision-making processes for attention to equity.
target_learners: K–12 education grantee organizations
target_learning_goals: Embedding equity in organizational learning and decision making
examples: The CBSL partnership applied this criterion in defining what counts as strong equity-centered strategic learning among pilot grantees.
key_sources: Emma Pottinger, Emily Gardner, Ramya Tallapragada, Alexandra Resch, Virginia Knechtel. (2021). Capacity Building for Strategic Learning: Findings from the Pilot Cohort. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/capacity-building-for-strategic-learning-findings-from-the-pilot-cohort

citation: Emily Gardner, Emma Pottinger, Ramya Tallapragada, Alexandra Resch, Virginia Knechtel. (2021). Capacity Building for Strategic Learning Using an Intermediary-Led Grantee Cohort Model: Recommendations for Funders. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/
title: Consider equity in both the organizational goal and the learning and decision-making approach
description: The article argues that strong equity-centered strategic learning requires equity to be embedded in how an organization learns and decides, not only in what it aims for. It states that "equity is considered in not only the organization's goal but also in its learning and decision-making approach," making the learning process itself an equity target.
requirements: Organizations must examine their learning and decision-making processes, not just their stated equity goals.
target_learners: K–12 education grantee organizations and funders
target_learning_goals: Embedding equity in organizational learning and decision-making processes
examples: The CBSL partnership adopted this stance as a criterion for what counts as strong equity-centered strategic learning among grantees.

article_title: Using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve math accessibility for students with visual impairments
citation: Kang Xue, Elizabeth Barker. (2022). Using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve math accessibility for students with visual impairments. https://www.nwea.org/resources/using-artificial-intelligence-ai-to-improve-math-accessibility-for-students-with-visual-impairments/
title: Assess item quality for accessible math tests by checking whether items measure achievement equally well for students with and without visual impairments
description: This principle defines item quality for accessible assessments in terms of equitable measurement: a high-quality item is "those that measured achievement for both students with and without VI equally well," while a low-quality item "showed differences between the two groups of students." The article applies this criterion to MAP Growth math items to separate items that work for screen-reader users from those that create barriers, framing accessibility as an equity issue in opportunity to learn math.
requirements: Achievement data from both students with VI taking accessible versions and students without VI taking standard versions
A method for detecting differential measurement between the two groups
constraints: Applied to math assessment items for students with VI who use screen readers; the brief does not claim generalization to other subjects or disability categories
target_learners: students with visual impairments
students without visual impairments
target_learning_goals: equitable measurement of math achievement
identifying assessment barriers for screen-reader users
examples: The study classified MAP Growth math items as high- or low-quality using this equal-measurement criterion across the two student groups
key_sources: Kang Xue, Elizabeth Barker. (2022). Using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve math accessibility for students with visual impairments. https://www.nwea.org/resources/using-artificial-intelligence-ai-to-improve-math-accessibility-for-students-with-visual-impairments/

article_title: Equity in the Driver’s Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education
citation: Babe Liberman and Viki Young, Ph.D. (2020). Equity in the Driver's Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Consultancy protocol in which a district team presents an equity challenge and peers probe it before offering suggestions
description: The article details a five-phase consultancy protocol: the district team presents its equity challenge for about ten minutes, consultants ask clarifying questions, then probing questions, then discuss the challenge in small groups while the district team listens, and finally the district team reflects and shares new thinking. Probing questions were 'deeper, open-ended questions that empowered the district teams to reflect on and think about collaboratively addressing their problem.' The protocol surfaced both common trends and context-specific observations about local policy, assets, and barriers.
requirements: A district team willing to present its equity challenge
Consultants who listen with dual purposes: helping clarify the challenge and generating their own ideas for tackling it
constraints: The authors state that in the future they would 'allow even more time for exploring and interrogating specific district challenges' and suggest probes to keep the group centered on equity
target_learners: District and school teams defining equity challenges, serving K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Clarifying and articulating equity challenges to generate relevant research questions and development priorities
examples: One district leader shared plans to use a consultancy protocol in her own district meetings after experiencing it at the convening
key_sources: Babe Liberman and Viki Young, Ph.D. (2020). Equity in the Driver's Seat: A Practice-Driven, Equity-Centered Approach for Setting R&D Agendas in Education. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/1185beda-6355-47f0-b3f2-980f6541172b

article_title: Partnering to promote equity and digital learning
citation: Wiley, K., Neisler, J., & Means, B. (2023, February). Partnering to promote equity and digital learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/167
title: Equitized syllabus with five equity characteristics
description: The report describes equitizing the course syllabus as a concrete equity mechanism taught in an ATD workshop and adopted by partner colleges. The equitized syllabus incorporates five characteristics: "Welcoming—Indicating that every student belongs in the class"; Representing Diversity through non-white and non-Western content, authors, or perspectives; Demystifying by communicating clearly about course expectations; Destigmatizing Support Services by describing them as useful for everybody; and Creating Partnership by portraying instructor and student as partnering for learning. BMCC standardized these syllabi across sections via a shared template.
requirements: Instructor participation in the Equitizing Your Syllabus workshop or equivalent guidance, and a shared template to standardize across sections
target_learners: Undergraduate students in high-enrollment gateway courses
target_learning_goals: Sense of belonging, clarity of course expectations, awareness of support services
examples: BMCC redesigned course syllabi based on principles from the Equitizing Your Syllabus workshop and created an equitized syllabus template shared with all faculty via Microsoft Teams
key_sources: Wiley, K., Neisler, J., & Means, B. (2023, February). Partnering to promote equity and digital learning. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/167

article_title: Designing a Process for Inclusive Innovation: A Radical Commitment to Equity
citation: Angevine, C., Cator, K., Liberman, B., Smith, K., & Young, V. (2019). Designing a Process for Inclusive Innovation: A Radical Commitment to Equity. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Two-by-two equity-innovation matrix for analyzing whether a solution is adapted or radical and who has access
description: The report offers a two-by-two matrix as a tool for analyzing innovation and equity in a given project or proposed solution. The x-axis indicates whether the project is closer to being adapted from something existing or closer to radical, i.e., significantly different and ready to scale; the y-axis analyzes who has access and whether access promotes equity or reinforces opportunity gaps. Inclusive Innovation seeks to move solution designs towards quadrants C and D, which are intentionally designed for the most marginalized.
requirements: Analysis of each project or proposed solution along both the innovation axis and the equity/access axis
target_learners: Education R&D teams designing solutions for marginalized populations
target_learning_goals: Designing solutions that are both novel and equitable in access and participation
key_sources: Angevine, C., Cator, K., Liberman, B., Smith, K., & Young, V. (2019). Designing a Process for Inclusive Innovation: A Radical Commitment to Equity. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/d6db3e76-2dc9-4ea6-ae68-49814c88e6b6

article_title: Using the EQUIP Observation Tool to Advance Equity in Math Classrooms
citation: Cunningham, J., Takahashi, S., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Using the EQUIP observation tool to advance equity in math classrooms. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: EQUIP observation tool for tracking and quantifying classroom participation patterns by demographic group
description: EQUIP (Equity Quantified In Participation) is an observation tool that helps educators "track patterns in student participation." Users upload a student roster with demographic information, optionally select discourse dimensions such as question types or talk time to cross-reference with demographics, and code each student contribution in real time or via video. The app then "automatically generate[s] analytics, including heatmaps, histograms, and various other data visualizations" that can surface participation inequities and prompt conversations about improving teaching practice.
requirements: Educators set up the app by uploading a student roster and associated demographic information they are interested in tracking
constraints: Discourse dimensions are optional; a user can simply record how many times a student participated
The report states the transformative power is not in the tool itself but in how it is used to enact change
target_learners: K-12 and community college mathematics students
target_learning_goals: equitable participation in classroom mathematics discourse
examples: A 1st-grade teacher's lessons were video-recorded and coded by researchers, who shared heatmap data reports in debrief conversations
A community college instructor used EQUIP six times in fall 2017 with a swivel camera and researcher coding
key_sources: Cunningham, J., Takahashi, S., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Using the EQUIP observation tool to advance equity in math classrooms. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655697

article_title: Using the EQUIP Observation Tool to Advance Equity in Math Classrooms
citation: Cunningham, J., Takahashi, S., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Using the EQUIP observation tool to advance equity in math classrooms. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Use EQUIP for teacher learning, not evaluation, and avoid reinforcing deficit views
description: The report advises that EQUIP's intended purpose is to support teacher learning: teachers must know they will not be evaluated or penalized based on data reports, and should have agency to choose the problem they work on. Users are also cautioned not to shift blame onto students, avoiding "want[ing] to fix students, rather than what kind of systems and structures are allowing students to participate or not."
requirements: Teachers need to feel safe to learn from the data
Professional development, protocols, and continued support to frame data use around growth rather than criticism
constraints: Without intentional steps to optimize learning and reduce harm, the tool's purpose is undermined
target_learners: K-12 and postsecondary mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: teacher learning about equitable participation
examples: The first PIRT debriefing focused only on positive feedback; later ones covered strengths and areas for improvement
Researchers emailed data reports in advance so teachers could process reactions independently
key_sources: Cunningham, J., Takahashi, S., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Using the EQUIP observation tool to advance equity in math classrooms. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655697

article_title: Engaging English Learners with Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics
citation: Haiwen Chu, Brent Jackson. (2024). Engaging English Learners With Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Equivalence reasoning progresses through three kinds of approaches — same value, related to each other, and transformable — across content strands
description: Across late elementary to middle grades, the brief organizes student approaches to equivalence in tables spanning fractions, rates, similarity of figures, algebraic expressions, and equations. Each strand is analyzed through the same three lenses: having the same value, being related to each other, and being transformable. As the brief puts it, "Table 1 presents some ways that students may reason about proportionality across the late elementary to middle grades," and Table 2 extends the same structure to expressions and equations.
requirements: Teachers should listen to students' reasoning across these approaches rather than requiring students to classify their own reasoning
constraints: The progression as printed spans late elementary through middle grades; high school work involves multiple representations across representational families
target_learners: late elementary, middle grades, and high school students, including English Learners
target_learning_goals: proportional reasoning, understanding the equals sign, equivalence of expressions and equations
examples: 4/8 and 2/4 are equivalent because they are both equal to 1/2 (same value); because 8 and 4 are twice 4 and 2 (related); or because multiplying 2/4 by 2/2 gives 4/8 (transformable)
key_sources: Haiwen Chu, Brent Jackson. (2024). Engaging English Learners With Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED671702

article_title: Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation
citation: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies
title: Treat equity for all students as fundamental to science education leadership
description: The framework's developers identified equity as the first shared value underlying the framework: all students should have access to education that prepares them for success, in student-centered environments with equitable, engaging, rigorous, and coherent opportunities. The article states "Ensuring equitable access requires educators to create the cultural and local relevance for students to engage in the practices and to understand the ideas of science," and leaders must recognize where inequity exists and find solutions to address it.
requirements: Leaders and educators must recognize areas where inequity exists and find solutions to address the inequity.
constraints: Equitable access depends on addressing environmental, cultural, and familial contexts of a wide range of students.
target_learners: All K-12 science students, with attention to economically disadvantaged students, students with disabilities, English language learners, and other groups named in the framework
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to rigorous standards-based science learning
examples: An elementary teacher leader refused to let students be pulled out for intervention during the science block, and the district mandated a science block so every child had access to science.
key_sources: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies

article_title: Getting Better at Getting More Equitable: Opportunities and Barriers for Using Continuous Improvement to Advance Educational Equity
citation: Valdez, A., Takahashi, S., Krausen, K., Bowman, A., & Gurrola, E. (2020). Getting better at getting more equitable: Opportunities and barriers for using continuous improvement to advance educational equity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Equity audits as a continuous improvement practice for seeing systems
description: Equity audits are a promising practice identified in the study for helping educators understand, or "see," their systems with a focus on "inequities in access, opportunity, and outcomes by student groups." TA providers and county offices of education use them to guide the collection and analysis of data, with results then used to inform improvement efforts. Topics vary by provider, from career and college readiness to discipline rates by student groups, and one county leader reported equity audits helped district leaders access in-school, in-classroom data beyond what the state dashboard provides.
requirements: Protocols vary by TA provider and focus area; audits require collecting data on differences in experiences, opportunities, and outcomes across student groups, including interviews with students
constraints: The dashboard alone does not provide the in-school, in-classroom view; audits complement rather than replace dashboard data
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly students of color and underserved student groups in California districts
target_learning_goals: Understanding and dismantling structural inequities in access, opportunity, and outcomes
examples: In 2018, San Rafael City Schools partnered with Education Trust West and the Marin Promise Partnership to conduct an equity audit of students' career and college readiness; one leader noted a reduction in suspension rates in one district
key_sources: Valdez, A., Takahashi, S., Krausen, K., Bowman, A., & Gurrola, E. (2020). Getting better at getting more equitable: Opportunities and barriers for using continuous improvement to advance educational equity. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606089

article_title: Reimagining Excellence: A Blueprint for Integrating Social and Emotional Well-Being and Academic Excellence in Schools
citation: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://selcenter.wested.org
title: Center equity in all aspects of a learning program, defined as comparably positive outcomes for all groups
description: The blueprint defines equity as "the attainment of comparably positive outcomes for all groups within, or served by, a program" and holds that equity exists when demographic characteristics are not predictors of outcomes. It directs that equity must be central to all aspects of a program — from leadership, professional learning, and instruction to digital inclusion, instructional materials, school culture, and relationships. Equitable programs build from the unique strengths and aspirations of students and provide the necessary support to overcome challenges.
requirements: An equity committee of diverse stakeholders that meets quarterly to establish a vision for program equity, lead the equity work, evaluate progress, and identify future priorities
An equity audit assessing the equity of services provided to student groups of interest and to teachers, staff, parents, and families
constraints: The blueprint warns that without addressing bias in the implementation of a multi-tiered system of support, schools may misinterpret student behavior and over-identify students for intensive support that they do not need
target_learners: Students of color, students learning English, students with disabilities, students from under-resourced communities, and all students served by the program
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to services and equitable opportunities for success across all program features
examples: The blueprint's equity audit covers policies and procedures affecting achievement, attendance, and discipline; program and classroom culture; instructional materials and assessments; professional learning; and stakeholder perceptions of equity, inclusion, anti-racism, and identity safety
key_sources: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613077

article_title: Educator Learning to Enact the Science of Learning and Development
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Flook, L., Schachner, A., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Cantor, P., & Osher, D.). (2021). Educator learning to enact the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/859.776
title: Guiding principles of equitable whole child design: five environmental features schools must provide
description: The report identifies five features of environments, structures, and practices attuned to students' learning and developmental needs: "positive developmental relationships," "environments filled with safety and belonging," "rich learning experiences that support deep knowledge development," development of social, emotional, and cognitive skills, habits, and mindsets, and "integrated support systems." Figure 1 presents these as the Guiding Principles of Equitable Whole Child Design, framed as transformative, culturally affirming, empowering, and personalized, sourced to the Learning Policy Institute and Turnaround for Children design principles.
requirements: School staff and leaders need a common knowledge base about child development across all domains to enact these features
constraints: The report notes these features are not easily achieved in factory-model school designs originating more than a century ago
target_learners: all K-12 students
target_learning_goals: healthy development, learning, and thriving through supportive school environments
examples: The School Development Program teaches all members of the school community to use principles of child and adolescent development to create a positive developmental environment
key_sources: Darling-Hammond, L., Flook, L., Schachner, A., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Cantor, P., & Osher, D.). (2021). Educator learning to enact the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/859.776

article_title: Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators
citation: Nicholas Munyan-Penney and Sarah Mehrotra. (2023). Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators. Ed Trust. https://edtrust.org
title: Four equity pillars framework for federal assessment policy
description: The report develops four "equity pillars" — ensuring consistent, high expectations for student success; encouraging relevant, inclusive assessments; providing timely, actionable, and easily accessible results; and making assessment results meaningful — as criteria for improving federal assessment policy. The pillars are grounded in the focus group findings and Ed Trust's equity-centered values, and are intended as a framework for forthcoming federal policy action including ESSA reauthorization. The report states the pillars "set clear priorities for what we believe should be the future of statewide assessments" and hopes they will be used by other advocates to assess future policy proposals.
requirements: Federal assessment policy proposals must maintain comparable, disaggregated statewide summative assessment data for the pillars to apply as intended
constraints: The framework addresses statewide summative assessments and federal policy, not classroom or local assessment design
The report notes faster results are in direct tension with developing more complex, authentic test items that take longer to score
target_learners: students of color
students from low-income backgrounds
students with disabilities
English learners
target_learning_goals: college and career readiness
equitable access to grade-level standards
examples: Pillar 3 cites Maryland releasing spring 2022 results in late January 2023, and suggests initial results be usable by educators while data-quality reviews are completed
key_sources: Nicholas Munyan-Penney and Sarah Mehrotra. (2023). Future of Assessments: Centering Equity and the Lived Experiences of Students, Families, and Educators. Ed Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628034

article_title: Next Generation Accountability: A Vision for School Improvement under ESSA
citation: Adams, C. M., Ford, T. G., Forsyth, P. B., Ware, J. K., Olsen, J. J., Lepine, J. A., Sr., Barnes, L. B., Khojasteh, J., & Mwavita, M. (2017). Next generation accountability: A vision for improvement under ESSA. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/next-generation-accountability
title: Educational Quality and Improvement Profile (EQuIP): a multi-indicator school reporting profile
description: EQuIP is the report's proposed accountability instrument, reporting data on school resources (organizational and home/community capacity), processes (instructional and learning capacity), and outcomes (cognitive and noncognitive). By reporting data on school resources, processes, and outcomes, "an EQuIP provides vital information for making judgments of school quality and helps focus school improvement efforts." It is envisioned as a comprehensive profile with multiple uses, with example pages for each capacity and outcome area and an online version (EQuIP Online).
requirements: Indicators should be collected with appropriate frequency and minimal disruption to the learning process
Indicators and measurement methods should have substantial evidence to support their validity and reliability
constraints: The report acknowledges no measure is perfect in its ability to accurately capture the phenomenon under study
target_learners: K-12 students
school stakeholders including parents, educators, and policymakers
target_learning_goals: deeper learning outcomes
college and career readiness
school quality improvement
examples: Example EQuIP pages are shown for organizational capacity, home and community capacity, instructional capacity, learning capacity, and cognitive and noncognitive outcome indicators
key_sources: Adams, C. M., Ford, T. G., Forsyth, P. B., Ware, J. K., Olsen, J. J., Lepine, J. A., Sr., Barnes, L. B., Khojasteh, J., & Mwavita, M. (2017). Next generation accountability: A vision for improvement under ESSA. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/next-generation-accountability

article_title: ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially intelligent multi-agent tutoring
citation: Solomon Sunday Oyelere. (2026). ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially intelligent multi-agent tutoring and participation-balanced collaboration in introductory programming. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100633
title: Operationalise equity in AI-mediated collaboration as participation balance and reciprocal engagement measurable from traces
description: In collaborative programming with AI support, define equity narrowly as trace-measurable properties of dyadic interaction rather than demographic outcomes. The article states "equity is operationalised specifically as participation balance and reciprocal engagement within dyads, rather than as demographic equity outcomes", captured through turn-share and word-share asymmetries, imbalance indices, peer-referencing, and reciprocal engagement rates. Analyses treat dyads as the substantive unit for participation-balance measures because such constructs are meaningfully defined at the group level.
requirements: Speaker attribution in logs (e.g., a speaker selector attributing messages to Student A or B) so turn-taking and participation can be reconstructed
constraints: This operationalisation avoids claims about fairness across demographic categories that the dataset cannot support; measures are behavioural proxies rather than latent learning
target_learners: Dyads of novice programmers in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: Balanced participation and reciprocal engagement within dyadic collaborative programming
examples: The benchmark includes measures of peer-referencing and reciprocal engagement designed to detect whether dialogue is structured as collaboration rather than parallel interaction with an AI tutor
key_sources: Solomon Sunday Oyelere. (2026). ASTRA: A synthetic benchmark for trace-based evaluation of socially intelligent multi-agent tutoring and participation-balanced collaboration in introductory programming. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100633

article_title: Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners
citation: Ashlyn Pierson, D. Teo Keifert, Bethany Daniel, Sarah Lee, Tessaly Jen, Adam Bell, Heather Johnson, Rachel Askew, Andrea Henrie. (2024). Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8
title: Two conceptualizations of equity: equity-as-access and equity-as-transformation
description: The article organizes its analysis around two conceptualizations of equity drawn from Grapin et al. (2023): equity-as-access, in which "learners should have access to disciplinary knowledge, practices, and career paths" (Grapin et al), and equity-as-transformation, in which "learners should transform what it means to learn and participate in disciplines" (Grapin et al). The authors use this distinction to diagnose why their initial PD design failed to disrupt deficit ideologies and to guide redesign. They cite a NASEM report arguing both are necessary, in which "equity-as-access supports short-term achievement, whereas equity-as-transformation disrupts systemic oppression in the long-term" (NASEM report).
requirements: Teachers and facilitators need explicit opportunities to distinguish and discuss both conceptions for transformative perspectives to emerge
constraints: The article reports relatively little research exists on equity-as-transformation, and notes the section is in the authors' discussion
target_learners: K-4 science teachers in professional development
target_learning_goals: Teachers' conceptualizations of equity in science teaching for multilingual learners
key_sources: Ashlyn Pierson, D. Teo Keifert, Bethany Daniel, Sarah Lee, Tessaly Jen, Adam Bell, Heather Johnson, Rachel Askew, Andrea Henrie. (2024). Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8

article_title: Experimental researches on learning to spell. Part I.
citation: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental researches on learning to spell. I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412810
title: Equal-difficulty word list methodology for classroom spelling experiments
description: The article describes a methodology for constructing and validating two lists of spelling words of equal difficulty for a given class. Words are selected from reading material slightly above the class level, tested by preliminary dictation, and confirmed as matched when averages are practically identical and the correlation between individual performance on the two lists is very high. This enables controlled comparison of teaching methods with actual school words rather than nonsense syllables.
requirements: Preliminary test must confirm equal difficulty: averages practically identical and positive correlation very high
Practice periods must be arranged so neither list has advantage in time of day or curriculum placement
Multiple practice sessions are needed; single practice exercises are unsafe
constraints: Lists suitable for one class may not be suitable for another even of the same standard or grade
Words must be ones no boy can spell entirely and most can partially accomplish
target_learners: elementary school children
target_learning_goals: correct spelling of curriculum vocabulary words
examples: Two 30-word lists were selected from a Standard III reading book for a Standard II class, tested by dictation on January 31st 1913, and confirmed as matched (averages 5.5 and 5.7, r = +.93)
key_sources: Winch, W. H. (1913). Experimental researches on learning to spell. I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412810

article_title: The measurement of ability in Latin. Part I. Vocabulary.
citation: V. A. C. Henmon. (1917). The Measurement of Ability in Latin. Part I. Vocabulary. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+Measurement+of+Ability+in+Latin%22+Henmon
title: Equal-step and equal-difficulty sublist construction for efficient vocabulary testing
description: A reusable test-design pattern in which a large scaled word list is decomposed into shorter instruments: a 25-word selected list whose words "decrease in difficulty progressively by fairly uniform steps, from the first year on," suitable across all four years, and four alternative lists (A, B, C, D) of 50 words each subdivided from the 200-word list so as to be of equal difficulty, with sums of scale values of 107.7, 107.9, 107.5, and 107.6. Standard scores for the 25-word list are printed by year (e.g. 13.7 number correct, 54.8 percent, for first year).
requirements: Prior scale values for every word so that sublists can be matched on difficulty
constraints: The selected 25 words were chosen to be neither too difficult for first-year nor too easy for fourth-year pupils
target_learners: first- through fourth-year high school Latin pupils
target_learning_goals: comparable vocabulary measurement across pupils, classes, and schools
examples: The 25-word list runs from accipio (average value 2.3) through vis (2.5), with per-year standard scores of 13.7, 18.6, 22.0, and 22.6 words correct
key_sources: V. A. C. Henmon. (1917). The Measurement of Ability in Latin. Part I. Vocabulary. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+Measurement+of+Ability+in+Latin%22+Henmon

article_title: Persistent association between family socioeconomic status and primary school performance in Britain over 95 years
citation: Sophie von Stumm, Sophie Nicole Cave and Paul Wakeling. (2022). Persistent association between family socioeconomic status and primary school performance in Britain over 95 years. npj Science of Learning (2022) 7:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00120-3
title: Equity versus equality in education as competing policy orientations
description: The article distinguishes two policy orientations: equality of education means "all children enjoy the same learning opportunities" — the same curricula, pace and methods regardless of ability — whereas "equity in education aims at reducing children’s differences in educational outcomes, by distributing education resources in ways that level the playing field for all children". The authors argue Britain's persistent SES–performance association reflects prioritising equality of opportunity over equity, and recommend redistributing resources toward children's differential learning needs.
requirements: Resource redistribution must be targeted at children with the greatest learning needs, for example by allocating more teaching staff to children at risk of academic failure and behavioural misconduct
constraints: The article notes equity prescribes inequality in educational opportunity, and that well-prepared parents who tend to occupy positions of power may object to redistribution; previous policies that maximised the best students' achievement, such as ability streaming or tracking, disadvantaged low-SES subgroups
target_learners: primary school children from low SES families
primary school children at risk of academic failure
target_learning_goals: reducing SES-related differences in primary school learning outcomes
weakening the intergenerational transmission of social and economic inequality
examples: The authors point to awarding grants to schools that enroll pupils from impoverished family homes to fund extra educational resources as an example of redistribution efforts
key_sources: Sophie von Stumm, Sophie Nicole Cave and Paul Wakeling. (2022). Persistent association between family socioeconomic status and primary school performance in Britain over 95 years. npj Science of Learning (2022) 7:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00120-3

article_title: An educational model of equity and computing: a study of marginalized student experience during COVID pandemic
citation: Li, Q., Moallem, M., Boettinger, J., Cai, Q., & Levi, M. (2024). An educational model of equity and computing: a study of marginalized student experience during COVID pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10443-0
title: Equity-5C (E-5C) model for computing education
description: The E-5C model is a prescriptive model aiming to achieve equity in computing education, grounded in social cognitive theory and social cohesion theory. The article states that "the model depicts five key elements (5Cs), communication, collaboration, confidence, curriculum, and career pathways, each represented by a circle," with computing equity at the center. The circular design reflects no hierarchy or fixed order, and double-arrowed lines indicate the elements may overlap and influence each other. The model guided the design of the Girls Who Code clubs and served as an advanced organizer for the ideas included.
requirements: Careful curriculum design grounded in evidence-based theoretical perspectives
Continued communication and interactions amongst stakeholder groups such as teachers/facilitators, students, and parents
constraints: The article states the model can be adapted for a virtual environment only with a slight modification of each element
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly girls and other underserved or underrepresented groups
target_learning_goals: Develop interest in computer science
Develop computational thinking skills
Promote equity in computing education
examples: The model was implemented in two Girls Who Code clubs (grades 3–5 and 6–12) on a university campus, using project-based learning with Scratch and later VexGo robotics
key_sources: Li, Q., Moallem, M., Boettinger, J., Cai, Q., & Levi, M. (2024). An educational model of equity and computing: a study of marginalized student experience during COVID pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10443-0

article_title: Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs
citation: Fink, M. C., Radkowitsch, A., Bauer, E., Sailer, M., Kiesewetter, J., Schmidmaier, R., Siebeck, M., Fischer, F., & Fischer, M. R. (2020). Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09876-0
title: In research programs on simulation-based learning, research and design should hold equal status and proceed iteratively rather than linearly
description: Building on the generic model for EDR, the article holds that "research and design coincide within at least a single phase of these programs, due to the custom development of complex products". An equal status of research and design is crucial when research materials and simulation components are developed and evaluated simultaneously, embedding design-and-construction and evaluation-and-reflection phases that may be iteratively repeated until all components are positively evaluated.
requirements: Programs must plan for multiple iterative cycles in which each cycle may focus on one or several components
constraints: Earlier phases are not necessarily executed as strictly separate, linear phases; one phase can start before another is completed
target_learners: researchers, designers, and content experts in educational research programs
target_learning_goals: creating effective research materials and simulations while generating scientific knowledge
examples: COSIMA 4 completed the construction and evaluation phase twice, revising prototypes after the pilot study before moving to empirical investigations
key_sources: Fink, M. C., Radkowitsch, A., Bauer, E., Sailer, M., Kiesewetter, J., Schmidmaier, R., Siebeck, M., Fischer, F., & Fischer, M. R. (2020). Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09876-0

article_title: Estimating the Effect of a Teacher Training Program on Advanced Placement® Outcomes
citation: Richard S. Brown & Emily Anne Brown. (2019). Estimating the Effect of a Teacher Training Program on Advanced Placement® Outcomes. International Journal of Computer Science Education in Schools, 2(4). https://www.csesjournal.org/
title: Equitable teaching practices plus resource-rich curriculum theory of teacher professional development
description: The article's underlying theory is that professional development enabling teachers with little computer science background to teach via equitable classroom practices, combined with a resource-rich curriculum, drives both overall learning and equity of participation. As printed: "teachers who engage students with equitable teaching practices coupled with a curriculum rich with resources and activities that support and encourage enactment of those practices will lead to (1) better student learning overall (2) more equitable student engagement and learning." The study's AP outcomes are treated as evidence consistent with this theory.
requirements: Teachers must be supported from the beginning to the end of the program, including facilitators trained in a year-long PD leadership program and Regional Partners building local sustainable hubs
constraints: The theory is tested here only on first-year AP test-taking and qualifying-score outcomes, not on attitudes, self-efficacy, or longer-term pursuit of computing opportunities, which the article names as future research
target_learners: High school students, including female and underrepresented minority students
target_learning_goals: Computer science learning and engagement
Equitable participation in computer science coursework
examples: Workshops devote time to reflecting on enacting equitable teaching practices in light of historic inequities faced by underrepresented groups in computer science
key_sources: Richard S. Brown & Emily Anne Brown. (2019). Estimating the Effect of a Teacher Training Program on Advanced Placement® Outcomes. International Journal of Computer Science Education in Schools, 2(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1207479

article_title: Testing the Efficacy of a Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention by Small Group Size
citation: Clarke, B., Doabler, C. T., Kosty, D., Kurtz Nelson, E., Smolkowski, K., Fien, H., & Turtura, J. (2017). Testing the efficacy of a kindergarten mathematics intervention by small group size. AERA Open, 3(2), 1–16. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858417706899
title: When small-group intervention formats produce equivalent outcomes, schools should consider the larger group size to serve more students within capped resources
description: The article argues that when two- and five-student intervention groups yield equivalent positive results, resource-based reasoning favors the larger group. In a district with capped Tier 2 funds, "Using a ROOTS grouping size of five would allow schools to serve 150% more students than if a two-student grouping was selected." The authors present this as a cost-benefit lens on intervention intensity decisions within multitier systems of support.
requirements: Evidence that the compared group formats produce equivalent outcomes, as established in this trial
constraints: Applies where monetary resources for Tier 2 services are capped; the article notes cost analyses do not include measures of benefit
target_learners: kindergarten students at risk for mathematics difficulties receiving Tier 2 services
target_learning_goals: whole number sense in early mathematics
examples: The authors contrast the two- and five-student ROOTS results from a resource standpoint, citing federal interest in cost analysis in IES efficacy grants
key_sources: Clarke, B., Doabler, C. T., Kosty, D., Kurtz Nelson, E., Smolkowski, K., Fien, H., & Turtura, J. (2017). Testing the efficacy of a kindergarten mathematics intervention by small group size. AERA Open, 3(2), 1–16. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858417706899

article_title: Study of the Effectiveness of Multi-Cultural Education on the Attitude towards National Integration of High School Students
citation: Shaheen Perveen. (2014). Study of the Effectiveness of Multi-cultural Education on the Attitude Towards National Integration of High School Students. li-manager's Journal of Psychology, Educational, Vol. 8 No. 2, August-October 2014. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Study+of+the+Effectiveness+of+Multi-cultural+Education+on+the+Attitude+towards+National+Integration%22+Perveen
title: Schools should integrate multicultural education into the curriculum and teachers should treat all students equally to promote unity in diversity
description: The article recommends that schools modify the curriculum to embed multicultural education and that teachers deal with all students objectively regardless of their own group membership. It states "The teachers in schools should treat all their students equally" and that "The school authorities should take an initiative in modifying the curriculum to integrate multicultural education in it", with classroom interaction compatible with promoting unity in diversity and open exchange of views to develop tolerance.
requirements: Teachers follow an objective approach in dealing with students
Institutions develop course content and related activities for impartial, secular and inclusive education
constraints: The study's own treatment showed no significant effect on attitude towards national integration, so the recommendation exceeds the demonstrated finding
target_learners: High school students in culturally diverse regions
target_learning_goals: Tolerance
Positive attitude towards national integration
Identification with each other across groups
examples: The article recommends scope for students to exchange their views openly and freely to develop tolerance

Study of the Effectiveness of Multi-cultural Education on the Attitude Towards National Integration of High School Students. li-manager's Journal of Psychology, Educational, Vol. 8 No. 2, August-October 2014. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Study+of+the+Effectiveness+of+Multi-cultural+Education+on+the+Attitude+towards+National+Integration%22+Perveen

article_title: Reflections versus Extended Quizzes: Which Is Better for Student Learning and Self-Regulation?
citation: Virginia Clinton. (2018). Reflections versus Extended Quizzes: Which is Better for Student Learning and Self-Regulation? Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning. https://doi.org/10.14434/josotl.v18i1.22508
title: Instructors can choose between brief quizzes with reflections and longer quizzes based on practical constraints, since both appear equally effective
description: Because the quasi-experiment found no learning or self-regulation advantage for either condition, the article advises that "quizzes and reflections appear to be equally effective and base their decision on what would work best for their particular learning environments". Instructors concerned about covering less content can be reassured, while those in large enrollment courses with minimal grading assistance may prefer longer quizzes, which can be automatically graded with feedback through learning management systems, since reflections may be labor intensive to grade.
requirements: Both methods require frequent, low-stakes assessment activities; the article notes quizzes and reflections were completed weekly online through the course learning management site with immediate feedback on quiz performance.
constraints: Findings come from a quasi-experiment in two large introductory psychology courses taught by the same instructor with identical lectures and exams; no passive control condition was included, so relative-to-nothing effectiveness is not established by this study alone.
target_learners: college students in large introductory courses
target_learning_goals: course content learning as measured by unit and final exams
metacognitive self-regulation
examples: The article notes an instructor who teaches large enrollment courses with minimal assistance for grading may appreciate that longer quizzes may be automatically graded with feedback through learning management systems, while reflections may be labor intensive to grade.
key_sources: Virginia Clinton. (2018). Reflections versus Extended Quizzes: Which is Better for Student Learning and Self-Regulation? Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning. https://doi.org/10.14434/josotl.v18i1.22508

article_title: A Joyful Classroom Learning System with Robot Learning Companion for Children to Learn Mathematics Multiplication
citation: Wei, C.-W., Hung, I.-C., Lee, L., & Chen, N.-S. (2011). A Joyful Classroom Learning System with Robot Learning Companion for Children to Learn Mathematics Multiplication. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Give every learner an equal, fair opportunity for hands-on practice with immediate feedback
description: The article's central design principle is that every learner should have an "equal opportunity" to participate and a "fair opportunity" of doing each hands-on practice, rather than a few students practicing at the blackboard while others watch. Equipping each learner with a robot learning companion and RFID input lets all learners practice simultaneously, retry several times, and receive immediate robot feedback, which the authors argue deepens impressions of the learning content and supports knowledge construction. The logged, summarised learning status also lets instructors adjust in-class strategy and give targeted after-school assistance.
requirements: One learning station per learner (RLC, RFID reader and tags, computation unit, display, network).
An instructor control station that logs activities and presents summarised real-time learner status.
constraints: The experimental group was limited to six students per round to maintain observation quality, so full-class deployment at scale was not tested in this study.
target_learners: elementary school children
target_learning_goals: mathematics multiplication
knowledge construction through hands-on practice
examples: In the experimental procedure, learners answered with RFID tags, were free to try several times, and the RLC spontaneously reacted with proper actions or sounds based on the inputs.
key_sources: Wei, C.-W., Hung, I.-C., Lee, L., & Chen, N.-S. (2011). A Joyful Classroom Learning System with Robot Learning Companion for Children to Learn Mathematics Multiplication. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ932221

article_title: Convincing Science Teachers for Inquiry-Based Instruction: Guskey's Staff Development Model Revisited
citation: Zambak, V. S., Alston, D. M., Marshall, J. C., & Tyminski, A. M. (2017). Convincing Science Teachers for Inquiry-Based Instruction: Guskey's Staff Development Model Revisited. Science Educator, 25(2), 108-116. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1143566
title: EQUIP (Electronic Quality of Inquiry Protocol)
description: The EQUIP (Marshall, 2009; Marshall, Horton, & White, 2009; Marshall, Smart, & Horton, 2010) was used to score each participant's instructional practices relative to IBI. The EQUIP measures the quality of IBI in regards to four components (i.e., instruction, assessment, discourse, curriculum) and provides a score for each of these constructs as well as an overall inquiry lesson score. Scores range from level 1 (pre-inquiry) to 4 (exemplary inquiry).
requirements: Researchers trained on the EQUIP observed participants' classrooms once prior to the PD, and at least once each 9 weeks during the academic year.
target_learners: in-service middle school science teachers
target_learning_goals: measuring the quality of inquiry-based instruction
examples: Marshall and Horton (2011) measured Cronbach alpha to be .92, .93, .85, and .81 for each construct respectively, and .94 for the overall lesson score.
key_sources: Zambak, V. S., Alston, D. M., Marshall, J. C., & Tyminski, A. M. (2017). Convincing Science Teachers for Inquiry-Based Instruction: Guskey's Staff Development Model Revisited. Science Educator, 25(2), 108-116. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1132092

article_title: Enhancing organizational health literacy through pediatric clinical training: Mini-CEX-based formative assessment in case-based learning for pediatric pneumonia-a perspective.
citation: Ge Sheng-nan, Li Bing, Mu Bing-yan, Wan Li-sheng. (2026). Enhancing organizational health literacy through pediatric clinical training: Mini-CEX–based formative assessment in case-based learning for pediatric pneumonia—a perspective. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1880936
title: Embedding equity-conflict scenarios into pediatric pneumonia case-based learning materials
description: The article embeds social-contextual variables with equity-conflict attributes directly into CBL materials for pediatric pneumonia. Teaching cases situate typical pneumonia presentations within composite backgrounds including "a primary caregiver who is a mother with limited health literacy, a dialect-based communication barrier, and a damp, crowded home environment lacking access to nebulization therapy", requiring residents to integrate biomedical and social-structural reasoning simultaneously.
requirements: Assessment anchors aligned with the conflict scenarios
Evaluators observe whether residents identify social obstacles and adjust management plans
constraints: Scenario backgrounds are composite rather than real patient cases
target_learners: pediatric residents
target_learning_goals: integrating biomedical and social-structural reasoning
designing context-sensitive care plans
examples: Cases include a caregiver with limited health literacy and no access to nebulization therapy, prompting alternatives such as equivalent non-nebulization plans
key_sources: Ge Sheng-nan, Li Bing, Mu Bing-yan, Wan Li-sheng. (2026). Enhancing organizational health literacy through pediatric clinical training: Mini-CEX–based formative assessment in case-based learning for pediatric pneumonia—a perspective. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1880936

article_title: USMLE Step 2 Clinical Knowledge performance by disability, race, and ethnicity in U.S. medical students: A multi-site study.
citation: Nguyen Mytien, Kim Michael, Pereira-Lima Karina, Hodgens Tiffany, Juliao Jordan, Holman Elizabeth, Sangsland J. T., Boatright Dowin, Meeks Lisa M. (2026). USMLE Step 2 Clinical Knowledge performance by disability, race, and ethnicity in U.S. medical students: A multi-site study. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0349774
title: Ensure equitable accommodation processes and supportive institutional practices when relying on high-stakes exam scores for selection
description: The article argues that as Step 2 CK gains weight in residency selection, programs and institutions must address structural barriers in assessment and accommodation processes. It warns that "Without parallel efforts to ensure equitable accommodation processes and supportive institutional practices, heightened emphasis on Step 2 CK may inadvertently perpetuate inequities that medical education has sought to mitigate." The principle calls for pairing any increased reliance on numeric scores with verified access to accommodations.
requirements: Accommodation processes that provide equitable access to high-stakes examinations for students with disabilities
constraints: The article notes Step 2 CK–specific accommodation data were not available, precluding direct examination of whether score differences reflect differential access to accommodations
target_learners: medical students with disabilities
URiM and Asian medical students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of clinical knowledge and clinical readiness in high-stakes licensing examinations
examples: The study found students testing without accommodations or with accommodations that do not fully address functional limitations, which the authors link to documentation gaps
key_sources: Nguyen Mytien, Kim Michael, Pereira-Lima Karina, Hodgens Tiffany, Juliao Jordan, Holman Elizabeth, Sangsland J. T., Boatright Dowin, Meeks Lisa M. (2026). USMLE Step 2 Clinical Knowledge performance by disability, race, and ethnicity in U.S. medical students: A multi-site study. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0349774

article_title: Connecting the dots: Examining stressful life events, campus climate, and school engagement on academic achievement and psychological distress in a predominantly Latine sample.
citation: Cruz, I. N., Moreno, K. A., Stovall, B., de la Vega, L. P., & Chavira, G. (2025). Connecting the dots: Examining stressful life events, campus climate, and school engagement on academic achievement and psychological distress in a predominantly Latine sample. Journal of Research on Adolescence, 35, e70096. https://doi.org/10.1111/jora.70096
title: Support historically marginalized adolescents exposed to stressful life events through equity-focused reforms that build school engagement
description: Because school engagement operated as the mechanism linking campus climate and stressful life events to achievement and distress, the authors recommend "intentional, equity‐focused reforms that address systemic barriers." Recommended practices include culturally responsive and trauma-informed pedagogy, restorative alternatives to exclusionary discipline, multilingual family partnership workshops, and recruiting and retaining diverse educators to strengthen belonging and climate.
requirements: Schools must foster student engagement, since a positive school environment alone may not improve academic outcomes unless it also fosters engagement
constraints: Findings are cross-sectional and from one predominantly Latine suburban high school; the authors call for longitudinal moderation analyses before stronger causal claims
target_learners: Historically marginalized adolescents in suburban schools exposed to stressful life events
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
Psychological well-being
School engagement and belonging
examples: The authors recommend culturally relevant pedagogy embedded in teacher preparation, trauma-informed professional development, restorative practices, multilingual family workshops, and diverse educator hiring
key_sources: Cruz, I. N., Moreno, K. A., Stovall, B., de la Vega, L. P., & Chavira, G. (2025). Connecting the dots: Examining stressful life events, campus climate, and school engagement on academic achievement and psychological distress in a predominantly Latine sample. Journal of Research on Adolescence, 35, e70096. https://doi.org/10.1111/jora.70096

article_title: Analysis of the applicability and utility of a gamified didactics with exergames at primary schools: Qualitative findings from a natural experiment.
citation: Quintas-Hijós Alejandro, Peñarrubia-Lozano Carlos, Bustamante Juan Carlos. (2020). Analysis of the applicability and utility of a gamified didactics with exergames at primary schools: Qualitative findings from a natural experiment. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0231269
title: Equip PE teaching places with digital technology and prepare installations in advance to support exergaming interventions
description: The article states that equipping the usual places where PE is taught with digital technology (projectors, Wi-fi) would solve the high demands to coordinate and plan spaces, since classes had to be given in each school's Assembly Room which is frequently requested by other teachers. Having installations previously prepared at the start of class, whenever possible, is believed necessary to create more student motivation and to optimize time. Seeking alternatives for the project to be consistent over time is necessary.
requirements: digital technology (projectors, Wi-fi) installed in the usual places where PE is taught
having the necessary time beforehand to adapt to the gamified exergame session
constraints: the logistics problem of spaces and installations cannot be completely solved by applying more coordination at school given its daily open dynamic character
target_learners: primary school students in Physical Education
target_learning_goals: sustained application of gamified exergaming interventions in PE
examples: At most schools in Spain, this intervention is applicable only by coordinating and managing spaces and materials well
key_sources: Quintas-Hijós Alejandro, Peñarrubia-Lozano Carlos, Bustamante Juan Carlos. (2020). Analysis of the applicability and utility of a gamified didactics with exergames at primary schools: Qualitative findings from a natural experiment. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0231269
